DESIGN OBJECTIVES(e2Awad)

The objective of this project is to create a dependable infant incubator system that maintains stable environmental conditions for premature infants. This is going to be done by maintaining precise temperature control and enabling effective monitoring. There will be a simulation prototype built using SciLab to test system interactions and to ensure temperature stability by using proportional control and PWM heating actions. The key parameters such as Kp for proportional gain, ADC sampling time and PMW heating action will be optimized. The simulation of the low-end prototype will be done using Proteus and Arduino-Uno to monitor heater air (ThA) and baby skin (ThB) temperatures via NTC thermistors. These reading will be displayed on 16x2 LCD display. An alarm will be triggered if the temperature of the baby skin (ThB) exceeds 37°C, the heater will stop if the heater air temperature (ThA) exced 37°C. Temperature readings and alarm status will be displayed on an 16X2 LCD screen. There will be a 9600 Baud, 8 data, no parity, one stop serial port provided by a PC running Node-RED, including a dashboard that visualizes the received temperatures ThA and ThB, the PWM level percentage, the alarm state, and transmit the desired body temperature (ThD). This web-based dashboard will be created using Node-RED for remote monitoring and control. This project aims to deliver a dependable and user-friendly solution that supports healthcare professionals in managing optimal conditions for infant care.

Overall system(özlem)

The overall system operates through the integration of both physical and cyber components, allowing for two-way communication between the incubator’s embedded system and the remote Node-RED dashboard. In the physical domain, the Arduino Uno is connected to two 4700 Ohm thermistors with a Beta value of 3900 NTC sensors, which are used to measure the air temperature (ThA) and the baby’s skin temperature (ThB). These thermistors are connected to the Arduino’s AD0 and AD1 pins. To verify data transmission, the Arduino's I01 serial data pin is connected to the RXD of a virtual terminal, enabling the transfer of data from the Arduino to the terminal.

Virtual communication between the Arduino and Node-RED is established through the Virtual Serial Port Emulator (VSPE), creating two virtual communication ports, COM10 and COM11. COM10 is used to interface with the Arduino, while COM11 is used for communication with Node-RED. This setup allows bidirectional serial data transmission between the two components. The Arduino receives data from Node-RED via its RXD pin (connected to COMPIM) and sends data to Node-RED through the TXD pin (connected to COMPIM(TXD)).

Data exchange is displayed in real-time on the Node-RED debug panel, demonstrating the successful communication link. To show the bidirectional data flow, a simulation is conducted where data from Node-RED appears on the Arduino virtual terminal, and data from the Arduino is shown on the Node-RED debug panel. Additionally, by interacting with the Button-TX in the Node-RED User Interface, the data from the button is displayed on the Arduino virtual terminal, confirming the two-way data flow between the system’s physical and cyber components. This entire setup demonstrates the seamless communication and control capabilities of the incubator system, facilitating real-time monitoring and adjustments via the Node-RED dashboard.

Introduction(Fazal-Mohammed)

The simulation of the Digi-Term System is the focus of this project; the work completed this semester incorporates the complete version of Digi-Term. The Digi-Term System is to be used to collect temperature data from the environment and display it on an LCD screen, the data throughput to occur at a specific baud rate. In this project, the Digi-Term System has the control feature on the presentation of temperature significant in baby care. This Cyber-Physical System (CPS) aims to ensure the baby’s body temperature (ThB) remains within safe thresholds of 32°C, 34°C, and 36°C, while an air heating system allows stable temperature control. The system measures both air heater (ThA) and baby skin temperature (ThB), ensuring ThB does not exceed 37°C, which could be life-threatening for infants. 

Using the Arduino Sketch coding language, the project will achieve three key objectives:

  1. Conceptual Simulation: A thermal system simulation to ensure stable temperature control.
  2. Low-End Controller Design: A cost-effective embedded controller using PWM to manage temperature efficiently.
  3. High-End Web Interface: A Node-RED web dashboard for remote monitoring and control, enabling healthcare professionals to adjust temperature settings and view real-time data.

Social impacts(Kardelen-Göktuğ-Alper)

Incubator system’s main purpose is to stabilize the vital functions of babies. They are easy to access for many people, which might help to reduce infant death rates, particularly in areas that have limited access to advanced healthcare services. Addition to that some diseases that may occur in babies in the future and are difficult to treat can be prevented by providing early care in an incubator. They also help for babies born with birth defects or those whose lives are in danger and provide mental support to parents by preventing them from falling into pessimism or hopelessness. Moreover, if they are used in care units provided free of charge by the state, incubators could be glimmer of hope many families and babies who do not have economic opportunities. Significant social impacts result from the incorporation of Internet of Things (IoT) technologies in incubators. Medical staff may spend more time to other important duties by automating routine operations and enabling remote monitoring, which raises the efficiency of healthcare as an entire profession. Plus, this innovation lowers the cost of operation, increasing the affordability of advanced incubator technology for patients and healthcare facilities because affordable solutions can lead to better outcomes for disadvantaged people and higher access to healthcare, the economic benefits often extend to society.

Design Requirements(Hisham,Omar)

We took these requirements from lab sheet[2]:

  1. Low-End System Requirements (Arduino UNO):

Microcontroller: Use an Arduino-Uno R3 with a 16 MHz clock.

Status Indicator: Implement a blink-alive LED on pin IO13, flashing every 400 ms every 5 seconds to indicate microcontroller status.

Temperature Sensors: Use two 4k7 NTC thermistors with a suitable linearization resistor to measure temperatures between 20°C and 45°C with a precision of less than 0.5°C. The thermistors should be able to calculate the temperature using the equation:

𝑇𝐾 = 1 𝑇𝑜 + 1 𝐵 𝑙𝑛 (𝑅𝑡 𝑅𝑜), where 𝑇𝐾 is in Kelvin (K).

AD Conversion: The ThA and ThB temperature sensors must be read every 50 seconds. During the development phase, a shorter sampling time of 5 seconds may be used for testing purposes.

Data Resolution: Store the temperature readings for ThA and ThB as 10-fold integers to maintain 0.1°C resolution (e.g., 32.6°C as 326).

Control Tasks: Implement proportional feedback control with a proportional gain (Kp) to regulate the heater. Every 10 seconds:

    1. Measure ThA and ThB.
    2. Calculate the error e = ThB – ThD
    3. calculate percent-Power, PP = Kp *e
    4. PWM period shall be 50 s. Duty time will be Td= 50*PP/100=PP/2 seconds
    5. keeps the heater output high for Td seconds.

An 16x2 LCD Display: Display should display the following values in a clearly recognizable format: For 0.1°C display resolution displays them as integers in 10 times scaled format, i.e., display 34.2 as 342.

i. Temperatures ThA and ThB (10 times scaled integer)

ii. ThD (desired-ThB) temperature (integer, {320, 340, 360}, represents {32, 34,

36} °C with one digit resolution after the decimal point.)

iii. Proportional gain Kp (integer)

iv. Alarm status: If air temperature ThA>37, make AA=1, else make AA=0,

v. When printing to the screen, try to alternate printing some variables in odd

seconds and other variables in even seconds so that the LCD screen flickers less.

The UART shall transmit 

The UART module in the system shall transmit the following data for monitoring and control purposes: 

i. Temperatures ThA, ThB, ThD

ii. Proportional gain Kp,

iii. Button SwCov (for cover status, low: cover closed, high: cover open),

iv. Alarm status AA (to display graphically the status of the incubator on the

NodeRED dashboard through transferring data to a PC).

v. UART transmission should stop and start when characters '(' and ')' are

received. M. Bodur 5.5. Infant Incubator Unit Structure 45. 

The UART Reception Requirements 

“(#p)”, and “(#d)” should assign the integer # to the parameters Kp, and ThD, respectively. Here, # denotes a decimal integer number. For example, “(15p)” means the received characters are {40,49,53,112,41}. These characters should accomplish the following actions: ‘(’ (C=40) stops transmitting characters, and initialize getting a decimal integer value, “15” specifies that integer is 15, “p” assigns 15 to 𝐾𝑝, and finally ‘)’ (C=41) starts the serial data transmission.

i. If the received ASCII character C is ‘(’, (C=40), transition on this guard should

accomplish a set action N=0, and SSP=1, which stops serial data transmission.

ii. When received character C satisfies 48 C 57, state transition should accomplish

a set action N=N*10+(C–48). For example, ‘1’ makes N=1, and ‘5’ after that ‘1’

makes N= 10*1+5=15.

iii. The characters ‘p’ (C=112) and ‘d’ (C=100) should accomplish set action to

assign Kp=N, and ThD=N, respectively.

iv. The last received character, C= ‘)’ should start serial transmission by the set

action SSP=0.

Modeling and analysis for conceptual design(i8-Göktuğ, t10-Alper, v5-Fazal)

To model Physical-Cyber Systems (CPS), we will utilize the Scilab XCOS environment to evaluate the potential performance of controls for the entire system. The following outlines the work we have done. For this part we had our own design and also compared from the Teams files provided.

Test A: Simulation of Physical system(Göktuğ)

We aim to determine the stable control law and parameters for the physical system. To construct the physical part of our CPS, Scilab XCOS offers a variety of palletes to simulate the system. From these, we used:

  • GAINBLK (Heater Temperature) with Gain = 30

This block multiplies the input signal by a factor of 30. It is used to scale a signal for the heater temperature to achieve the desired temperature ThD.

  • STEP_FUNCTION (25°C Environment), step time = 0, initial value = 0, final value = 25

Represents a step input signal that starts at 0°C and jumps to 25°C at time t=0.

  • SUMMATION with Datatype = 1, number of inputs = [1;+1], do an overflow = 0

Sums two inputs (positive and negative). The overflow option is disabled, meaning the sum is not restricted by maximum values.

  • SUMMATION with = 1, number of inputs = [1;+1], do an overflow = 0

Similar to the previous summation block.

  • Goto (ThA) with Tag visibility = 1

Used to route signals to a specified tag (ThA).

  • Goto (ThB) with Tag visibility = 1

Directs signals to the tag "ThB".

  • PULSE_SC with Phase delays = 100, Pulse width (% of period) = 5, Periods = 300, Amplitude = -10

Generates a pulse signal to generate square waves.

  • CLR (Air Heater) with numerator = 1, Denominator = (1+2*s)

Continuous-time block for a first-order system with a transfer function of 1/1+2s.

  • CLR (Chamber) with numerator = 1, Denominator = (1+30*s)

Another first-order transfer function, with a different time constant of 1/1+30s.

  • MUX with number of input ports or vector of sizes = 2

A multiplexer block that combines two input signals into one output. This is useful for selecting between two signal sources based on certain conditions or control logic.

  • CSCOPE with Ymin = 0, Ymax = 70, Refresh period = 550, Buffer size = 550

A display or scope block that plots the output signal in the range of 0 to 70. The refresh period and buffer size control how often and how much data is displayed, useful for real-time monitoring and analysis of the system's behavior.

The Scilab Xcos diagram in Figure 2 represents the physical layer of the Cyber-Physical System (CPS) of the Baby Incubator.

  • A constant Heater Temp (30°C) is provided as a control input and a 25°C Environment temperature acts as a baseline or external disturbance to simulate the real-world environment.
  • Next, the environmental temperature and heater temperature are combined in the Summation Block to compute the net input to the air heater.
  • The air heater's dynamics are modeled as a first-order transfer function representing its response characteristics.
  • The output of the air heater is summed again with another input to adjust the temperature entering the chamber.
  • The chamber dynamics are represented by another first-order transfer function. The response of this function is slower compared to the air heater.
  • Two outputs, ThA (air heater temperature) and ThB (baby temperature), are observed and passed through a MUX block for visualization on the scope.
  • The scope displays the behavior of the system, showing how the air heater and chamber temperatures evolve over time.

Explanation of Results:

Figure 3 shows the simulation of the system, where one can observe the dynamic relationship between air temperature ThA and baby skin temperature ThB. The heater is set at 30°C and the initial environment temperature is 25°C. The system underwent some minor disturbance in the simulation and went back to its steady-state temperatures.

ThA and ThB settle at steady state around 30° C. Observing the response curve shape:

  • The time constant of ThA is approximately 126s as it rises to 63% of its final value rather quickly.
  • The time constant of ThB is approximately 189s, reflecting the sluggish response owing to the thermal inertia of the baby skin relative to the air temperature.

The simulation confirms that ThA rises faster than ThB, showing the faster dynamics of heat transfer in the air heater compared to the chamber. These results validate the expected behavior of the modeled thermal system.

Test C: Simulation of added disturbance(Alper)

After performing the changes to the physical and cyber part of the CPS and verifying the results, the complete Signal Flow Diagram of the Baby Incubator is shown in Figure 10.

Observing the open-cover disturbance

Observing the open-cover disturbance in the closed loop test, we can see in Figure 9 that a pulse input has been applied at t = 200 s, resulting in an oscillating response from ThA and a more subtle one from ThB that reflect the expected dynamics of the system.

Analyzing various Kp values:

Observing the response in Figure 12, we can see as expected the ThA rises almost immediately as ThB starts decreasing due to the open cover of the incubator. With Kp = 1, the system reaches a steady state at approximately t=300s. At steady state ThA and ThB are equal and ThB = ThD as desired.

In Figure 13, as expected, the ThA rises almost immediately and ThB starts decreasing due to the open cover of the incubator, same as in Figure 10. However, now with Kp = 2, the system reaches a steady state at approximately t=340s as the system attempts to correct for the error in the response due to the increased gain of the PID controller. At steady state ThA and ThB are equal and ThB = ThD as desired.

Now we will test with Kp = 5. Figure 14 shows the system reaches a steady state at approximately t=400s as the system attempts to correct for the even larger error in the response due to the much-increased gain of the PID controller. At steady state ThA and ThB are equal and ThB = ThD as desired.

Finally, we test with Kp = 10. Figure 15 shows the system unable to reach a steady state as the system is unable to remove the error due to the very high Kp gain value. The baby temperature is unstable with this gain and is not acceptable.

Analysis of Test Results

Stability Analysis

The physical system modeling Test A shows that both ThA and ThB reach their respective steady-state values after a brief initial adjustment period. The following is observed from the test:

  • Open-loop scenario:
    • ThA reached the steady state faster with a time constant of about 126 seconds compared to ThB about 189 seconds. That agrees with the faster dynamics of the air heater when compared with the chamber and the baby's skin.
    • Both stabilized, meaning this system is stable in general.
  • Closed-loop tests in Test C:
  • If Kp=1 or Kp=2, the system was stable; it reached the steady state accordingly.
  • Whereas, for Kp = 5, it took little longer to stabilize with a larger oscillation before it settles.
  • Kp = 10, the system became unstable with heavy oscillations in ThB; this means very high gain values actually destroy the stability.

Offset Analysis

Offset is basically the difference between the desired set point temperature, ThD, and the stead-state temperature. Key observations are as follows:

  • For Kp = 1 offset was small, and ThB almost tracked ThD.
  • Larger gains like Kp = 2 slightly reduced the offset but resulted in slower stabilization.
  • For reasonable gain values, the offsets were negligible, which indicates that the proportional control mechanism was well-designed.

Ripple Analysis

Ripples indicate the variation of temperature about the steady-state value. The following were observed:

  • For smaller gains like Kp = 1 or Kp = 2, ripples in ThA and ThB were small and within permissible limits.
  • At Kp = 5, the oscillations became rather large, but were bounded in a post-settling steady state behavior.
  • With Kp = 10, the oscillations have become too large for the system to maintain a satisfactory temperature.

Conclusion of Analysis

This gives a Kp value between 1 and 2 as the best operating points for maintaining desired temperatures. We adjusted the Kp value as 1 to stabilize the baby’s temperature and we reduced the incubator temperature as 2 degrees. This maintains a good balance between stability, minimum offset, and low ripple. Gains outside this window compromise both performance and reliability of the system with increased oscillations that may lead to instability.

Prosis Simulation of the Low-End Design (i3-Kardelen, d1-Özlem, t9-Hisham, ve7-Mohammed)

In this lab, we designed and simulated a low-end temperature controller prototype, DigiTerm-05, using an Arduino Uno in Proteus-ISIS. The main tasks are configuring adjustable desired temperatures via UART commands, interfacing NTC thermistor sensors for real-time temperature measurement and conversion, and implementing proportional control using PWM to regulate the heating system. Key functionalities such as alarm states for exceeding safe temperature limits, data transmission to a PC for monitoring, and displaying critical parameters on an LCD were integrated. Also, we used the files from Teams that provided in this part. Here the general technical requirements [2] for this lab are:

i. has an adjustable desired temperature ThD. It is set through a

UART command.

ii. measures the voltages of two NTC thermistor sensor circuits:

ThA for heater air temperature, ThB for baby skin temperature.

iii. calculates temperatures ThA and ThB in Celsius, and displays the

temperatures ThA and ThB on a 2-line by 16-char LCD display.

iv. starts alarm state AA and stops heating if the temperature ThA

exceeds 37°C, and,

starts alarm state AB if the temperature ThB exceeds 37 °C,

v. Uses ThD to control ThB by proportional control action, with

PWM that switches the heater. In the control, ThA shall be

limited to maximum 37 °C

Arduino flashing light and serial output for debug(Özlem)

In this part, the system includes the integration of two 4.7K NTC thermistors, ThA and ThB, which will measure the air heater temperature (Ta) and the temperature of baby skin(Tb). We plan to connect these sensors to the Arduino Uno R3 board, which operates at a clock speed of 16 MHz, and linking them to analog pins AD0 and AD1, so we can obtain accurate temperature readings for monitoring and control purposes. Here some technical requirements[2]:

a. It must be developed on an Arduino-Uno r3 board with 16MHz

processor clock.

b. It must have a blink-alive LED (internal-LED of Arduino)

flashing for 400ms once at every five seconds.

We implemented and tested the flashing LED design to confirm its functionality using a finite state machine (FSM) on the Arduino Uno and I draw this FSM diagram for our system in figure 14. We can see it starts with OFF state and with initial tss=0 value and when tss reaches 5 seconds the LED is turned on for a duration of 400ms. When tss goes over 4 (meaning 400ms has passed), the FSM changes to the "LED OFF" state, turning off the LED until the cycle starts again.

I took the following code from teams provided project files:

Code:

// TEST-1 FlashLED and UART debug

//----------declarations-----------

int tss;

void FSM_flash(){

// FSM for flashing light.

tss++;

if(tss>=50) {

digitalWrite(13, 1); // Turn LED ON

tss=0;

Serial.print("A"); // Test of transmit "A"

}

if(tss == 4) { digitalWrite(13,0); } // Turn LED OFF

}

void setup () {

peripheral_setup();

// TODO: put your setup code here, to run once:

//----------setup-------------------

Serial.begin(9600);

pinMode(13,OUTPUT);

tss=0;

}

void loop() {

peripheral_loop();

// TODO: put your main code here, to run repeatedly:

//----------loop--------------------

delay(100); // 0.1-second loop

FSM_flash();

}

The FSM flashed the LED ON for 0.4 seconds and OFF for 4.6 seconds in a 5-second cycle, while transmitting the character "A" via UART at the start of each cycle. We configured the oscilloscope with a 200 ms/div horizontal sweep, 10 DC trigger level, and 2 V/div sensitivity to measure the LED signal.

In the figure 16 below, we observed via the virtual terminal that it takes 5 seconds for each A character to form. Additionally, the virtual terminal displayed "A" consistently at the correct intervals. This successful test verified the FSM's timing and UART transmission.

Figure 17 illustrates the oscilloscope output showing the blinking behavior of the LED controlled by the FSM_flash function. The waveform indicates that the LED turns ON for 400 milliseconds and remains OFF for the remaining 4.6 seconds of the 5-second period.

Possible measurement errors in our system include deviations in the LED flash timing. For instance, over a period of 300 seconds, the system is expected to flash the LED 60 times, as the LED flashes every 5 seconds. If the observed count were 59 flashes instead of 60, the error can be calculated as Error percentage=(Observed error/Expected Count)x100=1/60x100 and here Observed Error=Expected Count−Observed Count which is equal to 1.67% This 1.67% error accounts for a possible counting error during observation and the cursor for Oscilloscope cursor may have 0.1% error.

The experiment successfully met the technical requirements for this system. The FSM accurately controlled the LED flashing with the desired ON and OFF timings, and UART transmission of the character "A" confirmed this system’s functionality. We just had minor errors like 1.67% timing deviation(59 flashes in 300s) and a 0.1% oscilloscope cursor error and both errors are in acceptable limits so as a result we can say system was successful.

ADC of NTC sensor output (özlem)

In this part of the project, we integrated two 4.7K((4700 Ohm B= 3900) NTC thermistors to measure heater air temperature (Ta) and another parameter, such as a baby skin temperature (Tb). These sensors were connected to the Arduino Uno’s analog pins, A0 and A1, through voltage dividers with resistors. The Arduino’s ADC processed the signals, converting the sensor readings into temperatures using linear interpolation. Here some technical requirements[2]:
AD conversion of both NTC sensors (ThA and ThB) should be carried once at every 50 seconds. Readings of ThA and ThB should be represented as integers with 0.1 °C precision (i.e., physical ThA=32.6°C shall be represented as integer ThA=326). Arduino has an internal 𝑉𝑑𝑑=5V voltage regulator, and its ADC can use this supply voltage as 5V reference.

  • Sensors for temperatures ThA and ThB are two 4k7 NTC

thermistors with a suitable linearization resistor to read

temperatures between 20 … 45 degrees. ADC configuration

should provide sufficient dynamic quantization ratio to read the

sensor in full dynamic range ratio for the temperature range 20 …50 C.

The measured temperature values shall be used as integers

with 0.1 C precision, i.e., 37.5C should be stored and displayed as 375

Codes:

//----------declarations-----------

int tss;

int Ns0, Ns1, ThA, ThB, t50s;

int T1, T2, N1, N2, Tcr; // Calibration parameters for temperature calculation

void FSM_flash(){

// FSM for flashing light.

tss++;

if(tss>50) {

digitalWrite(13, 1); // Turn LED ON

tss=0; // Reset the counter

// Serial.print("A"); // Test of transmit "A"

}

if(tss == 4) { digitalWrite(13,0); } // Turn LED OFF after 400ms

}

void ADC_AB(){

// Default ADC resolution is 10-bit

// Read ADC, and Calculate Temperature

Ns0 = analogRead(A0); // Read the ADC value from sensor 1

ThA = 10.*T1 +Tcr+ (10.*T2-10.*T1)*(Ns0-N1*1.)/(N2-N1*1.);

// Linear interpolation to calculate ThA based on ADC reading Ns0

Ns1 = analogRead(A1); // Read the ADC value from sensor 2

ThB = 10.*T1 +Tcr+(10.*T2-10.*T1)*(Ns1-N1*1.)/(N2-N1*1.);

// Linear interpolation to calculate ThB based on ADC reading Ns1

}

void UART_printT(){ // Transmit ADC readings and calculated temperatures via UART

Serial.println();

Serial.print(" N0 ");

Serial.print(Ns0);

Serial.print(" Ta ");

Serial.print(ThA);

Serial.print(" N1 ");

Serial.print(Ns1);

Serial.print(" Tb ");

Serial.print(ThB);

}

void setup () {

peripheral_setup();

// TODO: put your setup code here, to run once:

//----------setup-------------------

// Initial setup for peripherals and variables

Serial.begin(9600);

pinMode(13,OUTPUT);

tss=0;

analogReference(DEFAULT); // Set calibration values for temperature calculation

//T1=20; N1=321; T2=50; N2=626; Tcr=0;

T1=20; N1=333; T2=50; N2=637; Tcr=5;

}

void loop() {

peripheral_loop();

// TODO: put your main code here, to run repeatedly:

//----------loop--------------------

delay(100); // Delay for 0.1 seconds

FSM_flash();

t50s++;

if(t50s >= 30) { // 500 for tasks at every 50 s.

// for faster debug purpose set t50s to 30.

t50s=0;

ADC_AB(); // Read ADC values and calculate temperatures

UART_printT(); // Transmit data via UART for monitoring

}

}

Procedure ADC_AB reads both of ThA and ThB sensors to Ns0 and Ns1, and calculates ThA = 10*ThA by linear interpolation.

Procedure UART_printT transmits the readings Ns0, Ns1, and, the calculated ThA and ThB values. We plan to use these values to make a plot of linearity for the sensors.

Figure 18 below shows the circuit for sensor interfacing and ADC. Two 4.7K NTC thermistors(RT1 and RT2) are connected to analog pins AD0 and AD1 of the Arduino Uno through 2.7K resistors (R5 and R6), forming voltage dividers. These allow the Arduino to read the resistance changes from the thermistors and convert them into temperature readings. I applied the values from lab sheet as RT1: 20°C and RT2 as 50°C.

Figure 19 displays the data transmitted via the UART to the virtual terminal. We can see the ADC values (Ns0 and Ns1) alongside the calculated temperatures. I observed that Ns0 is 333(ADC value for RT1 (20°C)) and Ns1 (637)( ADC value for RT2 (50°C)) and these values matches and close to lab sheet values. Also, we can see ThA(205) corresponds to 20.5°C which is close to the expected value of 20°C and ThB (505) corresponds to 50.5°C, which aligns with the expected 50°C. Our dynamic quantization ratio remains the same: DQ=N2−N1=637−333=304 and DQdB​=20⋅log10​(304)≈50dB. The dynamic range ratio of the NTC sensor for the same temperature is Ds=(50-20)/0.2=150 and in dB it’s equal to 43.5. So, I can say the ADC's dynamic range (304, 50 dB) is still higher than the sensor's precision range (150, 43.5 dB) like asked in the requirements, which indicates the quantization range error ratio of ADC is better compared to the sensor range precision ratio. As a result, we can say all readings align well with the expected values for 20°C and 50°C.

UART received character processing(Özlem-Mohammed-v4)

This part of the experiment includes the implementation of UART received character processing using an FSM (Finite State Machine) to handle commands sent through a virtual terminal. The primary goal is to update system parameters such as proportional gain (Kp) and desired temperature (ThD) based on user input, ensuring accurate and efficient command interpretation while ignoring invalid inputs. The FSM processes characters in real-time, providing seamless communication between the terminal and the Arduino system. Here some requirements according to lab sheet[2]:
Technical Requirements

  1. UART Command Parsing:
    • Commands follow the pattern (#d), where numerical values are parsed as integers and assigned to variables based on specific characters.
  2. Finite State Machine (FSM) Transition Rules:
    • Initialization:
      • When the received character is ( (C=40), initialize integer N=0 and stop serial transmission (SST=1).
    • Digit Handling:
      • If the received character is a digit (48 ≤ C ≤ 57), update the integer as N = N * 10 + (C - 48).
    • Variable Assignment:
      • For character d (C=100), assign ThD = N.
      • For character p (C=112), assign Kp = N.
  3. State Transition for Other Characters:
    • Characters not matching specific patterns, including ) or A, should:
      • Transition the FSM to the Ready state.
      • Reset serial transmission (SST=0).
  4. Handling ) in Ready State:
    • A ) character received in the Ready state should resume serial transmission by setting SST=0.
  5. Robustness to Invalid Input:
    • Any character outside the specified range or invalid sequence should not disrupt the FSM behaviour but transition to the Ready state.

In figure 22 shows that the system starts in the Idle state, where it waits for an opening character ( to begin processing a command. Once received, it transitions to the Accumulated Digits state, where it parses numerical digits (0-9) to form an integer. If specific command characters, like d or p, are received, it moves to the Command Processing state and assigns the parsed value to variables (ThD or Kp). Finally, upon receiving a closing parenthesis ), it transitions to the Command Executed state, completing the process. Invalid inputs at any stage return the system to the Idle state, ensuring robustness. This design efficiently handles UART command sequences while maintaining clear transitions for valid and invalid inputs.

We took code from the teams files:

void FSM_UART (){

// FSM for received character actions

C=Serial.read ();

while(C!= -1){

if(Su==0) { // Ready state handles initial characters

if(C==40) { // "("

N=0; SST =1; Su=1;} // Parses numerical input and assigns it to specific variables (ThD or Kp) based on subsequent characters.

if(C==41) { // ")"

SST =0; Su=0;}//")"

}else if(Su==1) { // numbr

if(C>47 && C<58) { // "0 ,... ,9" // If character is a digit ("0" to "9")

N=10*N+C -48;} // Update N with the new digit

else if(C==100){ // "d"

ThD=N; Su=0;} / Assign parsed value to ThD

else if(C==112){ // "p"

Kp=N; Su=0;} // Assign parsed value to Kp

else {SST =0; Su=0; } // unexpected char. Catch-all for undefined states

}else {Su=0;} // Transition back to Ready state

C=Serial.read (); }

}

The code reads characters from the UART buffer and performs specific actions based on the current state and the received character. The FSM starts in a “Ready” state (Su=0). When it detects ‘(‘, it initializes numeric accumulator (N=0), turns off the output (SST=1) and goes to state (Su=1). And if ‘d’ is received, it sets the value of (N) to ThD (desired temperature) or the stop Criterion value and returns back to the “Ready” state. If ‘p’ is received, it sets the value of (Kp) then returns back to the “Ready” state. Command End: Once it receives a symbol ‘)’, it turns to SST=0 bringing the system back to the “Ready” state for further serial transmission. Unrecognized characters bring FSM to the “Ready” state.

In figure 23 it shows the Arduino's TXD pin is connected to the RXD pin on the virtual terminal. This setup lets the UART work, making it possible to send data from the Arduino to the virtual terminal so we can monitor readings and parameters.

Control Task Implementation (Kardelen-Mohammed)

PWM and P controls are used in this system to manage the temperature of the incubator. P control generates the output "PP" (PP = Kp*e;) by scaling the error between the current temperature "ThB" and the desired temperature "ThD" (e = ThB – ThD) using a proportional gain constant "Kp" . "PP" has output that is limited to a acceptable duty cycle range, such as 1–99%. The PWM heater control operates in 0.1-second intervals, with the heater relay connected to IO12. Additionally, a 220Ω resistor and an LED were included as indicators for the heater's operation.

Technical requirements[2]:

For P control: ADC , NTC censors to keep parameters T1,T2 and Kp value.

For PWM control: tpwm to track cycle steps, LED, a pin to control LED, a condition to turn off the heater (Htr=0).

Heater OFF (OFF):
Transition from heater OFF to the heater ON state if the current time within the PWM period is less than the calculated on-time (on) and the air temperature (ThA) is below the overheat threshold of 37.0°C.
Heater ON (ON):
Transition from heater ON to the heater OFF state if the current time within the PWM period exceeds or equals the calculated on-time (on) or if the air temperature (ThA) reaches or exceeds the overheat threshold.
Overheat Protection (OVERHEAT):
Transition immediately to turn off the heater to prevent overheating when the air temperature (ThA) exceeds a safe threshold of 37.0°C.

Code for P Control and PWM:

void PControl (){

// PP is calculated at every 1minute.

PP = Kp * (ThD - ThB )/100;

if(PP >99) PP =99;

if(PP <1) PP =1;

//Limits PP to between 1 and 99

if(SST ==0){

Serial.print("␣PP␣");

Serial.print( PP );

Serial.print("␣"); } }

void FSM_PWM (){

// FSM for Controller output PWM at every 0.1s

tp2 ++;

if(tp2 >=2) { tp2 =0; tpwm ++; }

// Heater off regardless of Proportional control (over-heat protection )

if(ThA >=370) {Htr =0; }

if(tpwm >= 100) {

tpwm =0; Htr =1; Hto =0; }

// PWM cycle reset

if(tpwm == PP) {Htr =0; } // Cycle Check

digitalWrite (12, Htr ); // Output to LED

if(tp2 ==0 && SST ==0 && Htr != Hto ) {

Serial.print( tpwm );

if(Htr) Serial.print("h1␣");

else Serial.print("h0␣");

Hto=Htr;

// At the start of each PWM cycle , the state of the heater (Htr) is printed if it has changed from the previous state (Hto).

} }

UART connection(Hisham)

This lab is about improving UART data transmission to monitor and control system parameters like temperatures (ThA, ThB, ThD), gain (Kp), heater power (PP), alarm status, and cover status. We will implement some steps like updating the code and adding features like cover button status and alarm reporting, the system sends labelled data to a virtual terminal for real-time monitoring. With tests we check that data is sent correctly and the system works as expected in different situations.

Technical requirements[2]:

  • The overall system must be implemented correctly and functional
  • The cover switch status must be functional, and it must show when the lid is on or off
  • The alarm system must display an alert if the temperature for ThB is higher than 37.
  • The UART shall transmit the followings to the high-end device:
  • Temperatures ThA, ThB, ThD
  • Proportional gain Kp,
  • Button Bc (for cover position, low: cover closed, high: cover open),
  • Alarm status AA (to display graphically the status of the incubator on the NodeRED dashboard through transfering data to a PC).
  • UART shall receive the following ascii commands
  • “(#d)” for desired-ThB (denote it by ThD) values, where # can be any nonnegative decimal number.
  • “(#p)” for proportional gain Kp value, where # can be any nonnegative decimal integer number.

in order to improve the incubator controller's functioning, we add more sensor readings and report the cover switch state in this part by modifying the current code. The following revisions are among the modifications that enable us to report more comprehensive data via the Universal Asynchronous Receiver/Transmitter (UART) serial communication interface:

1: add cover switch status
To keep track of a cover switch's condition, we create an integer variable called SwCov. With a pull-up resistor, the switch is connected to pin 11 and is in input mode, which means that while it is open, it reads "high" (1) and when it is pressed, it reads "low" (0). The digitalRead() function is used to examine the status of this switch every 0.1 seconds. The status is sent via UART if it changes from open to closed or the other way around.

pinMode(11,INPUT_PULLUP); .

At every 0.1 second read the switch status by

SwCov=digitalRead(11);

and transmit

Serial.print(" C "); Serial.print(SCov);

2: Adjust the UART Output

UART_printAll() is the new name for the UART_printT() function. This function is in charge of using UART to transfer all required data. The following information is sent:

Sensor readings: ThA, ThB, and ThD temperatures.

Power Percent (PP): A percentage representing the current power output.

Alarm Conditions: It reports an alarm condition (AA0 or AA1 for ThA, AB0 or AB1 for ThB) if the temperature of either ThA or ThB over a threshold (369).

Cover Status: Whenever the cover switch's status changes, a message is received.

The code:

void FSM_PWM (){

// FSM for Controller output PWM at every 0.1s

tp2 ++;

if(tp2 >=2) { tp2 =0; tpwm ++; }

if(tpwm >= 100) {

tpwm =0; Hto =0; Htr =1;

if(ThA >=370) Hto =1;}

if(tpwm == PP) {Htr =0;}

if(ThA >=370) {Htr =0;}

digitalWrite (12, Htr );

if(tp2 ==0 && SST ==0 && Htr != Hto ) {

Serial.print( tpwm );

if(Htr) Serial.print("H1␣");

else Serial.print("H0␣");

// Output to LCD

lcd. setCursor (12 ,1);

lcd.print("H"); lcd.print(Htr );

Hto=Htr;

}

}

void UART_printAll (){

if(SST ==0){

Serial.println ();

Serial.print("Kp␣");

Serial.print(Kp);

Serial.print("␣Td␣");

Serial.print(ThD );

Serial.print("␣Ta␣");

Serial.print(ThA );

Serial.print("␣Tb␣");

Serial.print(ThB );

Serial.print("␣PP␣");

Serial.print( PP );

Serial.print("␣AA");

Serial.print( ThA >369 );

Serial.print("␣AB");

Serial.print( ThB >369 );

Serial.print("␣");

}

}

3: The Loop of Control and Reporting

To call UART_printAll() every minute (per 60 seconds), the loop is changed. It manages functions like data presentation, control logic updates, and sensor reading. Every 0.1 seconds, the status of the cover switch is checked; if it changes, the updated status is sent.

The code:

delay (100);

FSM_flash ();

t1m ++;

if(t1m > 59) { // tasks at every minute

t1m =0;

ADC_AB ();

PControl ();

UART_printAll ();

LCDdisp ();

}

FSM_UART ();

FSM_PWM ();

if(tp2 ==0) {

lcd. setCursor (8 ,1);

lcd.print("H"); lcd.print(Htr );}

oldSwCov=SwCov;

SwCov= digitalRead (11);

if(SwCov != oldSwCov ) {

Serial.print("␣C␣");

Serial.print(SwCov );}

For this test, we ran the simulation and observed the LCD display that’s shown in Figure 38. I tested the cover switch by closing it and opening it and it displayed the cover switch status to be functional in the terminal. I also tested the alarm status and increased the value for ThB above the threshold and it displayed the alarm.

Conclusion:

In this part, we improved the UART-based data transfer system for incubator parameters control and real-time monitoring. First, the existing code was modified; we added a cover switch status feature, then improved the alarm reporting, and finally ensured that all critical sensor data, including temperatures (ThA, ThB, ThD), power percentage (PP), and alarm conditions, were accurately transmitted. The modified system was then tested by running a simulation, which confirmed its ability to detect and report cover status changes (from open to close and vice versa). When the cover is open, the system triggers a cooling effect due to heat loss, requiring the controller to compensate by increasing the heater's duty cycle to maintain stable temperatures. Conversely, when the cover is closed, the system reduces heat loss, stabilizing the internal environment and reducing the heater's workload. Additionally, the system triggers an alarm when the temperature of the baby (ThB) exceeds 37 °C. All these improvements helped in the reliability of the incubator controller, ensuring better monitoring and response to environmental conditions.

Node-Red Dashboard Implementation(d6-Omar,it3-Kardelen,ve2-Awad)

Components for a Real-World Physical Prototype(Kardelen)

For this part of the project, the goal was to connect an Arduino UNO to a host system running Node-RED software by serial connection. Since it can link with many kinds of sensors, the Arduino UNO is a versatile and cost-effective microcontroller that runs well in straightforward data gathering and control applications. Alternatively, a PC or Raspberry Pi board may serve as a high-performance host controller, giving substantial computing power for complex data integration and processing along with comprehensive connection options like Ethernet, Bluetooth, and Wi-Fi.

Visual Terminal was added to display the output of data from Ardunio and COMPIM. Also AND gate, U2.A(74HC08), is used to regulate signal transitions or control in serial communication. 

COMPIM was added to enable communication with systems in the outside world through the virtual circuit through the ports. COMPIM settings should be edited to: Physical port COM10, Physical Baud Rate 9600, virtual baud rate 9600.Figure 40 shows that the necessary values are entered.

Data from Arduino's TX pin goes to COMPIM's RX pin and is directed to the computer's COM port. Data from the computer is transmitted from COMPIM's TX pin to Arduino's RX pin. Thus, bidirectional serial communication is established between the Arduino and the computer (or the terminal on Proteus). All the parts were combined and turned into a single Arduino base.

After checking the Node-Red and VSPE test parts, a single dashboard was created by bringing together all the circuits made on Proteus to connect the main system to Node-Red. That dashboard is shown in Figure 42.

VSPE

In order to connect the system to the user interface, a connection must be established between NODE RED and PROTEUS through ports. These ports were created through VSPE.

  • The first port is called COM10 as the connector
  • The second port was created as a connector with the name COM11
  • A serial redirector was added to connect these two ports.

Dashboard Flow Diagram

In our Node-Red flow chart , at start I used a Serial In which is connected to Arduino COM11, our proteus output is shown as :

I am using 8 functions to (parsing) break the output we got from serial in (proteus) like in this function:

Function to Show Kp:

if (msg.payload && typeof msg.payload === 'string') {

    let data = msg.payload.trim();

    let parts = data.split(", ");

    let kpPart = parts.find(part => part.startsWith("Kp:"));

    if (kpPart) {

        let kp = kpPart.split(": ")[1];

        msg.payload = parseFloat(kp);

    } else {

        node.error("Kp data not found in the payload", msg);

        msg.payload = null;

    }

} else {

    node.error("Invalid or undefined payload", msg);

    msg.payload = null;

}

return msg;

Other 7 functions do the same exactly , but for different input values : ThD , Cover Status , ThA , ThB, PP , AA and AB. Each function will deliver each output value which will be sent to nodes connected to it.

- “Format Kp” Function:

if (msg.topic === "Kp") {

msg.payload = "(" + msg.payload + "p)";

}

return msg;

-This function formats the user's input that they control using the Slider node to adjust the proportional control factor (Kp). It checks if the topic is "Kp", if true, it formats the payload into the required syntax. For example, if the user inputs 5, the function formats it as (5p) to set Kp = 5.

-“Format ThD” Function:

if (msg.topic === "ThD") {

msg.payload = "(" + msg.payload + "d)";

}

return msg;

- This function formats the user's input that they control using the Slider node to adjust the desired Temperature (ThD). It checks if the topic is "ThD", if true, it formats the payload into the required syntax. For example, if the user sets slider as 37, the function formats it as (37d) to set ThD as 37.

Dashboard Organization

At first when we started designing the dashboard , the most important requirements to fulfill is a friendly user interface which is easy to use , we achieved this requirement by labelling everything on the dashboard and made sure that we use clear fonts to easy vision for user. Second requirement is to have an organized dashboard that user can see and control everything as needed seamlessly.

We fulfilled these requirements by firstly , as shown in this Figure 46 , divided the dashboard into 6 main groups : Settings , Baby Temperature , Air Temperature , Percent Power Display , Cover Status and Control. Settings group on dashboard will just display ThA,ThB,ThD,Kp,PP in text to achieve a user-friendly interface. In Baby Temperature group , it will show a thermometer , a chart and a gauge to show the baby’s skin current temperature. Same for Air Temperature , PP , cover status and Control.

In Control Group, the user can control desired Kp and ThD as needed , it will be shown in a text and a gauge with colors to show ThD level.

Overall test of the system(Awad-Hisham)

Technical requirements:

  • The system must have a functional LCD display that shows the different temperatures.
  • The system must show the cover switch status
  • The system must show percentage power
  • The system must allow for configuration to the temperature values
  • The system must have a functional connection between low-end and high-end.

The LCD display was tested using different ThA and Thb, the initial temperature for ThA was set to 38°C and ThB as 39°C and the where displayed correctly on the LCD display as shpwen in the figure above. In the first test the cover opened. Then ThA was changed to 32°C and ThB to 31°C again the LCD passed the test as everything was correctly shown, and the cover closed.

The dashboard was tested to see if it displays the correct outputs on the dashboard, ensuring the connection between the low-end and the high end, and also to test the overall work of the system and ensuring the system is maintaining the desired temperature of the baby. As seen in the above figure as the temperature of the baby exceeds the desired level the percentage power of the heater decreases to 1%.

Here we can also see as the temperature of the heater air goes above 37°C the cover is on (1) and the pp decrees to the minimum possible value, this is done to decrees the temperature of the air inside the incubator to make sure the baby’s stays in the safe zone.

Overall, the system has successfully passed all major tests, from LCD display to the control logic and safety mechanism. It accomplished the overall objective of maintaining the baby’s temperature within a safe range while providing a real-time monitoring and feedback through the dashboard and LCD display. The system demonstrated its safety mechanism successfully, by closing and opening the cover automatically according to the requirements of the situation, while also lowering and increasing the temperature of the heater air (ThA) and percentage power (PP). All the test showed how the integration between components is robust, and how the system effectively adapts to varying conditions to prioritize safety and stability.
